evidence.claim: Forest highways and surviving concrete trace western Arkansas’s changing road network
evidence.quote: Much of the Byway lies within the Ouachita National Forest.

evidence.claim: surviving concrete trace western Arkansas’s changing road network
evidence.quote: It is concrete pavement 18 feet (5.5 m) wide with no shoulder, and there is a single concrete slab bridge, which spans Bear Creek. This roadway section was built 1927–29, when US 71 was first built. It was bypassed in 1959.

evidence.claim: The West–Northwest Scenic Byway is a network of connected highways: 261 miles designated an Arkansas State Scenic Byway in 2005.
evidence.quote: Designated as a State Scenic Byway in 2005, the West-Northwest Scenic Byway is comprised of 261 miles of interconnected highways

evidence.claim: Much of it lies within the Ouachita National Forest, with U.S. 71 running north from Mena and Highway 10 extending between the Oklahoma line and Ola.
evidence.quote: including Highway 71 from Mena to I-540 and portions of Highway 10 from Ola to the Oklahoma State Line and of Highways 23 and 96. Much of the Byway lies within the Ouachita National Forest.

evidence.claim: Highway 10 crosses mountainous terrain near Havana and Belleville.
evidence.quote: Highway 10 begins to cover mountainous terrain, passing Havana, Belleville, and the Danville Municipal Airport.

evidence.claim: Highway 10 began as one of Arkansas’s original state highways in 1926 and remains close to that early routing.
evidence.quote: Highway 10 was one of the original 1926 Arkansas State Highways, and remains very close to that routing today.

evidence.claim: Near Jenny Lind, a surviving stretch of U.S. 71 shows another stage of road building: narrow concrete pavement laid in 1927–29.
evidence.quote: It is concrete pavement 18 feet (5.5 m) wide with no shoulder

evidence.claim: It was bypassed in 1959.
evidence.quote: This roadway section was built 1927–29, when US 71 was first built. It was bypassed in 1959.

evidence.claim: The 2005 byway designation joined these highway corridors with portions of Highways 23 and 96.
evidence.quote: including Highway 71 from Mena to I-540 and portions of Highway 10 from Ola to the Oklahoma State Line and of Highways 23 and 96.

evidence.claim: concrete pavement laid in 1927–29.
evidence.quote: This roadway section was built 1927–29, when US 71 was first built.

evidence.claim: For the Mena-to-Ola journey, head north through the forest toward Waldron, which the U.S. 71 mainline bypasses to the west.
evidence.quote: US 71 runs north through the forest to Waldron, a town the mainline route bypasses to the west

evidence.claim: Continue through Mansfield toward Greenwood, with Jenny Lind farther north.
evidence.quote: North of Waldron, US 71 passes through Mansfield and Greenwood

evidence.claim: Return toward Greenwood for Highway 10 east past Fort Chaffee, Booneville and Magazine, then continue through Havana, Belleville and Danville to Ola.
evidence.quote: The highway leaves town and passes Fort Chaffee on its way to Logan County.

evidence.claim: Jenny Lind farther north.
Highway 10 east past Fort Chaffee, Booneville and Magazine
evidence.quote: In Booneville, the route intersects the scenic Highway 23 near the Bank of Booneville Building and Farmers and Merchants Bank-Masonic Lodge. Highway 10 also passes the Booneville Municipal Airport before entering Magazine.

evidence.claim: continue through Havana, Belleville and Danville to Ola.
evidence.quote: Highway 10 begins to cover mountainous terrain, passing Havana, Belleville, and the Danville Municipal Airport. Highway 10 intersects Highway 27 in Danville and Highway 7/Highway 28 in Ola.

evidence.claim: Mena grew with the Kansas City, Pittsburg and Gulf Railroad, whose trains began serving the town in 1896.
evidence.quote: Mena was founded by Arthur Edward Stilwell during the building of the Kansas City, Pittsburg and Gulf Railroad (now the Kansas City Southern), which stretched from Kansas City, Missouri, to Port Arthur, Texas. Train service to Mena began in 1896.

evidence.claim: Founder Arthur Edward Stilwell named it for Folmina Margaretha Janssen-De Goeijen, his financier’s wife, called Mena by her husband.
evidence.quote: Stilwell named the town in honor of Folmina Margaretha Janssen-De Goeijen, the wife of his friend and financier Jan De Goeijen, whom Mr. De Goeijen affectionately called Mena.

evidence.claim: The railroad’s departure from its local shops in 1910 cost the town eight hundred jobs.
evidence.quote: In 1910, the railroad moved its shop facilities from Mena to Heavener, Oklahoma. This created a loss of eight hundred jobs.

evidence.claim: The route through Mena passes the Kansas City-Southern Depot and the commercial historic district.
evidence.quote: In Mena, US 59/US 71 has a brief overlap with Highway 8, during which the routes pass two NRHP listings, the Mena Kansas City-Southern Depot and the Mena Commercial Historic District.

evidence.claim: Southeast of Jenny Lind, an old stretch of U.S. 71 survives as Doraul Acres Lane.
evidence.quote: The Old US 71-Jenny Lind Segment is a stretch of historic road pavement southeast of Jenny Lind, Arkansas. It consists of a bypassed section of U.S. Route 71 (US 71) that is now designated Doraul Acres Lane.

evidence.claim: Its concrete pavement is eighteen feet wide, without a shoulder, and a concrete slab bridge crosses Bear Creek.
evidence.quote: It is concrete pavement 18 feet (5.5 m) wide with no shoulder, and there is a single concrete slab bridge, which spans Bear Creek.

evidence.claim: Built in 1927–29 and bypassed in 1959, the segment preserves an earlier highway alignment.
evidence.quote: This roadway section was built 1927–29, when US 71 was first built. It was bypassed in 1959.

evidence.claim: Nearby Jenny Lind took its name from the Swedish opera singer.
evidence.quote: The community was named for Jenny Lind, a Swedish opera singer.

evidence.claim: Coal discovered in the 1880s brought a new mining settlement beside the older community; the mines closed in the 1950s.
evidence.quote: Coal was discovered in the area in the 1880s, and a mining community known as New Jenny Lind was established adjacent to the former settlement

evidence.claim: the mines closed in the 1950s.
evidence.quote: The mines, upon which the local economy was dependent, closed in the 1950s.

evidence.claim: Camp Chaffee’s first soldiers arrived on December 7, 1941, the day Japan attacked Pearl Harbor.
evidence.quote: The first soldiers arrived on 7 December 1941, the day of the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, Hawaii.

evidence.claim: Armored divisions trained here during World War II; the installation also held 3,000 German prisoners of war.
evidence.quote: from 1942 to 1946, the 6th, 14th and 16th Armored Divisions trained there.

evidence.claim: Renamed Fort Chaffee in 1956, it briefly received Elvis Presley in 1958.
evidence.quote: On March 21, 1956, the name of Camp Chaffee was officially changed to Fort Chaffee

evidence.claim: During his four-day stay, Presley received his first military haircut in Building 803.
evidence.quote: For four days in 1958, Chaffee was home to Elvis Presley, who as part of his induction into the Army received his first military haircut in Building 803.

evidence.claim: In 1975–76, Chaffee processed Vietnamese and Cambodian refugees, and the Arkansas National Guard now uses it for training.
evidence.quote: from 1975 to 1976  it was a processing center for refugees from Southeast Asia and held Vietnamese and Cambodian refugees after the Vietnam and Cambodia wars.

evidence.claim: the installation also held 3,000 German prisoners of war.
evidence.quote: Fort Chaffee also served as a prisoner-of-war-camp during World War II, housing 3,000 German prisoners of war.

evidence.claim: the Arkansas National Guard now uses it for training.
evidence.quote: the Arkansas National Guard has been using 66,000 acres (270 km2) as a training facility.

evidence.claim: At Greenwood, the connection between the old and new roads survives in Highway 10 Spur. Until the mid-1960s, that road was part of U.S. 71’s original alignment; it now connects U.S. 71 west of town with Highway 10 near downtown.
evidence.quote: Its western terminus is at US 71, just west of Greenwood, while its eastern terminus is at Highway 10 near downtown Greenwood. Until the mid-1960s, this road was part of the original alignment of US 71.

evidence.claim: Janssen Park, in the center of town, also bears her name.
evidence.quote: Janssen Park in the center of Mena is also named for her.

evidence.claim: Mena was incorporated in September 1896, and two years later the county seat moved here from nearby Dallas.
evidence.quote: Mena was settled in 1896 and incorporated on September 18 of that year. In 1897, the Bank of Mena was founded. The following year, the county seat was moved from nearby Dallas to Mena.

evidence.claim: The new settlement was originally called New Jenny Lind, while its neighbor became Old Jenny Lind; the newer community eventually shortened its name.
evidence.quote: a mining community known as New Jenny Lind was established adjacent to the former settlement, which became known as Old Jenny Lind (also known as Altus and Old Town). Eventually the name of New Jenny Lind became shortened to just Jenny Lind.

evidence.claim: Its later history also includes sheltering people displaced by Hurricane Katrina in 2005, when empty barracks became temporary housing.
evidence.quote: In September 2005 Fort Chaffee housed evacuees after Hurricane Katrina struck Louisiana. The empty barracks were converted into temporary housing

flags: ARDOT’s 261 miles describes the full network; material maps 155.9 miles and supplies strip towns only for the US 71 arm. Narrative uses Mena-to-Ola direction, reversing strip-mile direction on US 71; Jenny Lind requires returning toward Greenwood before continuing east. Fort Chaffee remains a separate excursion, with its exact current title and coordinates retained.

Dropped current claim that the Ouachitas are North America’s only east-west mountains. ARDOT says this but supplies no corroboration; its adjacent byway description uses a different geographic scope. Also omitted its unsupported causal generalization about terrain suiting settlers.
Current Jenny Lind distance dropped: cache says about 0.75 miles, not an exact three-quarters of a mile. Other retained current claims are supported; highway-speed comparison omitted as unnecessary.

Fort Chaffee cache distinguishes the training installation from redeveloped land but provides no reliable current visitor-access procedure for Building 803. No access or building-survival promise made; no notice or practical directions added. Cache gives no drive time.
